youtube.baslik: First Fit and Fine-Tuning by Patient Complaint | Lesson 193 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
How do we solve complaints of muffled, metallic, echoey or own voice sound after a hearing aid is fitted? In this lesson we cover the first fit, acclimatization, linking complaints to frequency regions and input levels, and the logic of step-by-step fine-tuning.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Dillon, Hearing Aids; Mueller, Ricketts and Bentler, Modern Hearing Aids; Jenstad, Van Tasell and Ewert (2003), Hearing aid troubleshooting based on patients' descriptions, Journal of the American Academy of Audiology; American Academy of Audiology, Guidelines for the Audiologic Management of Adult Hearing Impairment.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about the day the aid is first fitted, and fine-tuning based on the user's complaints at later visits.
We will link muffled, metallic, echoey and own voice complaints to frequency regions and gain.
The first fit begins by checking the physical fit of the aid in the ear: is it comfortable, does it stay in place, is there leakage?
The person inserts and removes the aid themselves a few times; if this step is skipped, many later complaints come from here.
The audiogram, age and hearing aid experience are entered correctly in the software, and a prescriptive formula is chosen.
The aid's feedback path is measured by the software, so the cancellation system is tuned to that ear.
Then match to target is verified with real-ear measurement.
Finally, insertion, cleaning, batteries or charging, and what to expect in the first weeks are explained.
A first fit that goes well markedly reduces the complaints met at later follow-up visits.

maddeler.metin: Lower starting gain for new users

cumleler: The brain's adaptation to sounds heard again is called acclimatization.
In first-time users, especially with moderate and severe loss, starting gain may be kept somewhat below target.
Many fitting programs offer the option of raising gain over the weeks, automatically or step by step at follow-up visits.
In the first days, rustling paper, running tap water and footsteps may sound unusually loud and artificial.
Some of these are environmental sounds that have not been heard for years but are actually normal.
The most effective way to acclimatize is to use the aid regularly all day, not only in difficult settings.
Users describe their problems not in technical terms but in their own words; troubleshooting starts with these words.
Expressions such as muffled, blocked or like cotton wool are often heard.
Some users find sounds metallic, tinny or like a robot's voice.
Many also describe hearing their own voice as echoey, as if they were talking inside a barrel.
A sharp, piercing or shrill discomfort is a different group of complaints.
Everything being too noisy, or sound being heard but not understood, are also common complaints.
The first step of fine-tuning is to work out which acoustic problem these words correspond to.
Most complaints can be roughly linked to a frequency region.
Muffled, echoey and own voice complaints are often related to the low-frequency region, roughly below 750 Hz.
Complaints that speech sounds nasal or as if it comes from a box are often linked to the mid frequencies.
Metallic, sharp or crackly sounds, or piercing sibilants, usually point to the high-frequency region, above 2000 Hz.
But the same word can mean different things to different people; muffled can also come from too little high-frequency gain.
So the map is a starting point; the decision is made with measurement and together with the person.
Now let us gather common complaints with possible causes and example adjustments in a table; these are examples, not fixed recipes.
With a muffled complaint, high-frequency gain may be too low or low-frequency gain relatively high; usually high-frequency gain is raised.
With a metallic or tinny complaint, high-frequency gain may be too high; it is reduced, or the lows are raised slightly.
With an echo complaint about own voice perception, occlusion is considered first; the vent is enlarged or low-frequency gain reduced.
Discomfort with loud sounds may show that gain for high inputs, or the maximum output level, is too high.
Not hearing soft sounds, on the other hand, points to too little gain for soft inputs.
Difficulty in noise is not always a fitting problem; noise programs, directional microphones and realistic expectations go together.
Measuring again after each adjustment makes sure that solving the complaint does not cost speech audibility.
In compression hearing aids, gain can be adjusted separately for each input level.
This graph shows, as an example, the aid's output in the ear canal as a function of input level.
If the person says they do not hear whispers or distant speech, gain can be raised for soft inputs only.
In the blue curve, output for soft inputs has risen, while output for loud inputs has not changed.
This adjustment makes soft sounds audible without increasing discomfort from loud sounds.
Conversely, if only loud sounds are bothersome, gain for loud inputs is reduced and soft inputs are left alone.
The top line is the maximum power output, or MPO; this level must not exceed the person's discomfort level.

ogeler.metin: Does the person turn it down?

cumleler: At a follow-up appointment, the aid's data logging helps in understanding the complaint.
Data logging shows how many hours a day the aid is used and in which sound environments the person spends time.
If the person keeps turning the volume down, overall gain or gain for loud sounds may be too high.
A program that is never used is either unnecessary, or the person does not know how to switch to it.
Some aids can learn from the person's volume preferences and change gain over time; this change is also tracked in the log.
Short wear time may signal discomfort, expectations or a physical problem; always ask why.
In this example, both ears show a symmetrical loss sloping toward the high frequencies; the person is a first-time user.
In the second week, they say that the clatter of cutlery and their own voice sound metallic.
On real-ear measurement, average speech matches target, but at high inputs the high-frequency output is slightly above target.
In this example, only the high-frequency gain for loud inputs can be reduced by a few decibels; average and soft inputs are left alone.
The person is told that acclimatization is ongoing and that high-frequency gain will be reviewed again in a few weeks.
This way comfort is achieved and the high-frequency consonants of speech are not lost.
The first step is to make the complaint concrete: when, where, with which sound and talking to whom does it bother the person?
The second step is to rule out physical causes: earwax, a blocked filter, a wrongly inserted earmold or the wrong program.
In the third step, only one thing is changed at a time, in small steps, for example a few decibels.
Changing several parameters at once makes it impossible to know which one worked.
In the fourth step, the result is checked with real-ear measurement, making sure audibility is not lost while solving the complaint.
In the last step, the change and its reason are recorded; at the next visit, the person is asked about its effect.
This cycle can sometimes take several appointments; patience and regular follow-up are part of success.
The solution to some complaints lies not in the software but in the earmold; the vent, earmold length or dome type can be changed.
Separate programs for music, noise or the phone help people for whom one setting does not suit every environment.
A wrongly inserted earmold or dome can cause both muffling and whistling; insertion training is repeated.
If the limit of adjustment has been reached for noise and distance, assistive devices such as remote microphones are recommended.
Finally, talking about the gap between what is expected of the aid and what is possible eases many complaints without any adjustment.

maddeler.metin: Fine-tuning may move away from target

cumleler: Every adjustment made for a complaint can move the aid somewhat away from the prescriptive target.
Small deviations for comfort are normal; the problem is when deviation makes important parts of speech inaudible.
So after the adjustment, look at the speech map and check whether the high-frequency consonants are still above threshold.
When the target is deliberately departed from, the reason is written in the file.
This way another clinician can also understand why the fitting is the way it is.
Once the person has acclimatized, bringing the reduced regions back toward target can be tried.

sahneler.metin: Write down the complaint in the person's own words, with the moment it happened. If possible, recreate a similar sound in the clinic, adjust with it, then verify with measurement.
cumleler: A tip from the field: note the complaint in the person's own words, together with the concrete moment they experienced it.
Saying "plates in the kitchen really pierce my ears" gives much more information than saying "sounds bother me".
If possible, recreate a similar sound in the clinic; for example, use jingling keys or a recorded environmental sound.
Try the adjustment together while this sound plays, and ask the person about the difference.
Then verify the change with real-ear measurement, because not every setting that sounds good is the right setting for speech.

maddeler.metin: One change, small steps, measure again
Not every complaint is solved by settings

cumleler: In this lesson we saw that the first fit is completed with physical fit, verification to target and user orientation.
Muffled, metallic, echoey and own voice complaints can be roughly linked to low, mid and high frequency regions.
In fine-tuning, one change is made at a time, steps are kept small and the result is measured again.
Earmolds, programs, training, assistive devices and expectation counseling are also part of fine-tuning.

sahneler.soru: A person says sounds are metallic. What comes to mind first?
sahneler.aciklama: Descriptions like metallic and tinny often point to _too much gain in the high frequencies_; the result is checked by measurement.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: a user says sounds are metallic and tinny. Which possibility comes to mind first?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: too much high-frequency gain.
This description often points to too much high-frequency gain; adjust in small steps and check with the speech map.
